questions.question: A tariff protects home producers by ...
options: taxing imports at the border so their shelf price rises
limiting the number of units that may enter the country
paying domestic firms a production grant
rationing foreign currency to importers

questions.question: Why do economists distrust quotas even more than tariffs?
options: Quotas raise government revenue too quickly
Quotas hand out import licences that become private prizes for favoured firms
Quotas only apply to agricultural goods
Quotas lower prices for consumers

questions.question: Dumping is best defined as ...
options: selling surplus stock at a discount in the home market
importing goods without paying tariffs
exporting at below cost or below the home price, often to destroy competitors before raising prices
refusing to export a strategic product

questions.question: Protection is 'politically easy and economically expensive' because ...
options: voters usually oppose tariffs
producers pay for the protection themselves
the state receives no revenue from tariffs
gains concentrate loudly on protected producers while losses spread thinly and invisibly across all consumers

subtopics.title: The Case for Protection Against the Case for Free Trade

questions.question: The standard rebuttal to the infant-industry argument is that ...
options: protected infants rarely admit to growing up, so shelter without expiry breeds permanent inefficiency
young industries never need any help
infant industries only exist in rich countries
tariffs cannot legally protect new industries

questions.question: Why can protecting jobs in one industry destroy jobs elsewhere?
options: Because protected workers usually emigrate
Because dearer protected inputs burden downstream producers, and retaliation kills export jobs
Because protection reduces the population
Because tariffs lower the exchange rate

questions.question: Which is the strongest, least contested argument for protective action?
options: Raising general state revenue
Guaranteeing profits for large firms
Anti-dumping action against predatory pricing from abroad
Keeping all consumer prices high

questions.question: The 'desirable mix' of trade policy is best described as ...
options: complete free trade with no exceptions ever
high walls around every domestic industry
protection for whichever industry lobbies loudest
broad openness plus rare, temporary, conditional protection with a written expiry

subtopics.title: Export Promotion, Import Substitution, and South Africa's Path

questions.question: Import substitution industrialises by ...
options: replacing imports with home production behind tariff walls
subsidising firms to sell abroad
eliminating all trade barriers
importing only capital goods

questions.question: Why do industries raised behind high walls tend to stay small and inefficient?
options: Because their workers lack skills
Because the home market is their ceiling and the wall removes pressure to match world costs
Because banks refuse to lend to them
Because they export too much

questions.question: Export promotion offers which advantage over import substitution?
options: It guarantees the home market to local firms
It removes the need for infrastructure
The world market has no ceiling, so scale economies open and world competition forces efficiency
It protects the economy from world demand swings

questions.question: South Africa's export performance today is throttled mainly by ...
options: the world's highest tariff walls
a ban on manufactured exports
a shortage of trade agreements
logistics and electricity constraints — the ports, rail and power behind the border

subtopics.title: Globalisation, the WTO and the Ladder of Integration

questions.question: The World Trade Organisation was created in 1995 out of ...
options: the GATT process, after the Uruguay Round of negotiations
the African Continental Free Trade Area
the Southern African Customs Union
the European Union's founding treaty

questions.question: The most-favoured-nation principle requires that ...
options: rich countries pay for poor countries' imports
a trade benefit granted to one partner extends to all members
each country favours its oldest trading partner
tariffs rise equally for everyone

questions.question: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: Free movement of labour and capital
A shared currency
A common external tariff charged to non-members
The absence of internal tariffs

questions.question: The AfCFTA is the continent's wager that ...
options: tariffs between African states should rise
Africa should trade only with the global north
each African economy grows fastest alone
a single market of over a billion people can let African industries outgrow small national ceilings

subtopics.title: The Chip Stall and the Hawkers at the Rank

questions.question: Charging every hawker R30 a day to trade at the fence is the rank's version of ...
options: a tariff
a quota
a subsidy
exchange control

questions.question: Why do the four licensed hawkers become defenders of the licensing rule?
options: They admire the chip stall
The licence itself is now worth money to those who hold it
They prefer paying fees
The rule lowers their prices

questions.question: Demanding health certificates from the fence hawkers but not from the stall mirrors which trade barrier?
options: An export incentive
A customs union
Standards applied more zealously to outsiders
A most-favoured-nation clause

questions.question: Protecting the stall saves two visible jobs but costs two thousand commuters R2 more each day. This illustrates ...
options: that protection benefits everyone equally
that consumers gain from tariffs
that hawkers cause unemployment
protection's arithmetic: concentrated visible gains, thinly spread losses that add up to more

subtopics.title: Raising the Young Stall Without Spoiling It

questions.question: The new chip stall deserves temporary shelter because ...
options: it is a genuine infant whose costs will fall with scale once it learns and grows
all stalls deserve protection permanently
commuters prefer expensive chips
the hawkers are breaking the law

questions.question: The 'hammock danger' describes what happens when ...
options: shelter expires too soon
protection without expiry removes the pressure to improve, so the infant never grows up
hawkers undercut the stall
the stall expands to other ranks

questions.question: Which THREE rules keep infant-industry protection honest?
options: Permanent shelter, no targets, cover every firm
Secret shelter, high fees, old firms first
A written expiry date, performance pressure, and genuine infants only
Subsidies, quotas and bans together

questions.question: The stall's two futures — selling only to this rank forever, or supplying ranks across the city — represent ...
options: dumping and anti-dumping
tariffs and quotas
globalisation and autarky
import substitution and export promotion

questions.question: The metro-wide agreement letting any vendor trade at any rank with no fees between ranks is the analogy for ...
options: a free trade area, like the AfCFTA
an economic union, like the EU
exchange control
a dumping duty

questions.question: Adding one identical entry fee for OUTSIDE vendors turns the arrangement into ...
options: a common market
a customs union, like SACU
a free trade area
a most-favoured-nation treaty

questions.question: In the referee's rulebook, 'once a vendor is inside your gate, treat her like your own' mirrors ...
options: bound tariffs
dispute settlement
the national treatment principle
export promotion

questions.question: The honest four-part summary of globalisation from the rank is ...
options: bigger markets, no losers, perfect rules, equal gains
smaller markets, more fees, fewer lunches, better rules
closed gates, cheaper lunches, no referees, no arguments
bigger markets and cheaper lunches, real losers deserving real help, and a rulebook forever arguing with itself
